messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 59
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Professor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Stress: Stress
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 59-year-old professor of African diaspora studies at a mid-sized university, a man whose life had been defined by intellectual order and the quiet authority of a lecture hall. He came to therapy not because he wanted to, but because his department chair had noticed him flinch and freeze during a routine faculty meeting when a colleague mentioned a weekend trip to a lake. That single word—*lake*—had sent a cascade of sensation through him: the smell of damp earth and silt, the cold weight of water, the sound of nothing but his own heart. He had excused himself to the bathroom and stood gripping the sink, waiting for his body to stop shaking. It never truly did.

The trauma that dismantled him happened two years ago, on a research trip to his home country. Kwame had taken his younger brother, Kofi, to visit the coastal village where their grandmother had lived. Kofi was not a strong swimmer, but the water that afternoon looked deceptively calm—a broad, slow river meeting the sea. Kwame had turned away for no more than a minute to photograph a distant fishing boat. When he looked back, Kofi was gone. There was no cry, no thrashing. Just a sudden, silent absence where his brother had been standing waist-deep. Kwame ran into the water, but it was murky and cold, and he could not see. He dove and groped blindly, his lungs burning, until fishermen pulled him out, gasping and empty-handed. Kofi’s body was recovered three days later, tangled in submerged roots downstream.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame returned to the United States and tried to resume his life. He taught his classes, graded papers, attended department events. But the world had become a place of hidden traps. The first time it happened, he was walking across campus after a rainstorm and stepped onto a flooded patch of sidewalk. The sight of standing water—brown and leaf-littered—sent an electric jolt through his chest. Before he could think, *This is just a puddle*, his legs had locked, his breath had stopped, and he was standing frozen, staring, while students streamed around him. He had come to believe that his body knew danger before his mind did, and that this was not a symptom but a truth: the water was always waiting. He began to avoid the campus pond, the fountain in the quad, the aquarium in the student union. He stopped walking near the river trail he had once loved. When a colleague offered him a ride home in the rain, he lied and said he had errands, then stood under an awning for forty minutes until the downpour stopped, because the thought of sitting in a car while water drummed on the roof made his stomach turn.

The smells were worse. A student once walked into his office carrying a bag of takeout—fried fish—and Kwame had to excuse himself mid-sentence. The odor of river water, of damp reeds and silt, seemed to cling to certain foods, certain cleaning products, even the air after a heavy rain. He began to keep his office window closed year-round. He stopped eating fish entirely. He told himself it was a dietary choice, but he knew the truth: he could not bear the way that smell pulled him back underwater, blind and frantic, searching for his brother.

Over months, the avoidance narrowed his life. He stopped attending department socials because they were held near the campus lake. He declined a prestigious conference in New Orleans because the hotel was on the river. His relationships frayed; friends stopped inviting him to barbecues or beach trips, tired of his excuses. He was certain that people thought he was aloof or difficult, but what frightened him most was the feeling that he was never truly safe. Even in his own apartment, far from any body of water, he could not relax. He would sit on his couch, lights on, television playing, and still his shoulders would be tight, his jaw clenched, as though the flood might come through the walls. He had begun to dread the end of the workday, because at home there were no lectures to distract him from the watchfulness.

What finally brought him to seek help was a morning in late spring. He had woken from a nightmare—the same one, always: his hands in murky water, grasping at nothing—and found himself standing in his bathroom, fully dressed, at 4 a.m., ready to go check on Kofi. For a long moment, he did not know where he was. The grief and the guilt and the fear had fused into a single, suffocating certainty: that he had failed his brother, that he should have been able to save him, that the water was still there, waiting, and that no amount of vigilance would ever make it safe. He called the university counseling center that morning. He was not sure what he hoped for—perhaps only that someone might tell him how to stop feeling like he was still drowning.
